name: pattern-matching
intent: Eliminate a value drawn from a closed set of variants by matching its structure and binding the payload, so the compiler proves that every variant is handled before the program runs.
problem: Code that inspects which variant of a tagged value it received - a result type, a domain event, an AST node, a protocol frame, a state - drifts into chains of type tests, casts and accessor calls, and nothing guarantees that a variant added later is handled: the missing branch is found in production rather than by the compiler.
context: Applies when a value's type is a closed sum - an enum with payloads, a sealed hierarchy, a discriminated union, a tagged union - and behaviour depends on which variant arrived. It needs a match construct (language syntax, a variant type with visitation, or a type-level bottom-type check) plus a compiler or checker able to see the set as closed: same-unit sealing, private constructors, or explicit non_exhaustive / @unknown markers where a set is published to other teams.
benefits: Totality is proved at build time: an unhandled variant fails the build at every dispatch site, moving the failure mode from production to the compiler.
Destructuring removes the classic boilerplate: no casts, no instanceof chains, and for a closed set no per-operation visitor classes.
Adding a variant becomes a guided refactor: the compiler lists every site that must decide about the new case.
Data and behaviour stay separable: variant types can live in a data module while operations live where they are used, so adding an operation touches no existing type.
Layered and recursive data is expressed directly - record, sequence, mapping and nested patterns describe the shape instead of a hand-written traversal.
Everyday sum types (Option/Result/Either, state machines, protocol frames) become safe by construction: absence, failure and protocol alternatives cannot be ignored silently.
Each arm is an independent case with its bindings in scope, which keeps matching functions locally readable and easy to test.
tradeoffs: A wildcard, else or default arm silently disables the coverage proof for every future variant - the cheapest-looking edit destroys the property the pattern was adopted for.

The proof exists only while the set is visibly closed, and sealing is language-specific: sealed/permits inside one compilation unit, private constructors, enum classes, or non_exhaustive markers at library boundaries. Open hierarchies get a runtime throw instead of a proof.
Coverage is a warning by default in several ecosystems (C# CS8509, Scala E029, GCC -Wswitch), so the guarantee is only load-bearing once warnings-as-errors is configured.

Adding a variant is a source-breaking change across every match site by design; for a published API that cost trades against compatibility, which is why forward-compatible sets need explicit opt-outs.
Arm order is semantics: first match wins, so an earlier broad pattern makes later arms unreachable, and guarded arms are excluded from coverage analysis because a guard may be false.
Compilation of matches is not free: simple tag switches become jump tables, but deep patterns with guards fall back to sequential tests, which can show up in hot paths.
Nullable and absent values are separate cases: coverage over the non-null type does not cover nil/null/None, and that extra arm is easy to omit where the checker does not demand it.
Stale artefacts still fail late: an exhaustive match compiled against an older sealed set can throw at run time, so the guarantee is compile-time only and must be re-established by recompiling.
A large match can decay into switch soup, re-centralising behaviour that polymorphism would keep local, and making merges and reviews harder as the variant set grows.

participants.responsibility: The value being matched: one instance of the closed variant set, usually passed by value or by reference without any downcast.
The closed alternatives (enum cases, sealed subtypes, union members), each carrying exactly the fields valid for it and no others.
A structural test plus binders - constructor, record, sequence, mapping, constant, type or relational pattern - that matches one shape and extracts its parts.
Selects the first arm whose pattern and guard accept the subject, evaluates order, and produces the result value of the operation.
An optional side condition evaluated after the pattern has bound its variables; it refines an arm but never counts towards coverage.
Whatever makes user-defined types matchable: extractor objects (unapply), deconstruct/deconstruct_keys, __match_args__, Deconstruct, property patterns, or a discriminant property.
The compiler or type checker that decides whether the arm set covers the closed variant set, reports the missing case, and fails (or warns) before the program runs.
The wildcard/else/default arm that catches everything the other arms miss; it makes the match total at run time while removing the compile-time coverage proof.

use_cases: Interpreter and compiler front ends: expression and statement types are evaluated with one total match per operation, and a new node kind cannot be forgotten.
Protocol and RPC dispatch: a frame or command is one of a fixed set of shapes, and each shape is deconstructed into its fields instead of being cast.
Result and error mapping at boundaries: translating domain failures into transport errors, where every failure variant must be given a mapping.
State machines and workflow states: states carry state-specific data, and transitions are written as a total match over (state, event) pairs.
Domain-event handling in reducers and event-sourced aggregates, where every event type must be applied to rebuild state.
Command-line and query parsing: token or request shapes are matched structurally, including literals and sequence patterns, before validation logic runs.
OpenJDK Java 21 sealed hierarchies: pattern switches over AST or domain-event variants can enumerate permitted types without a default, using the compiler's exhaustiveness analysis.
rustc and Rust enum APIs: match expressions destructure enum variants and the compiler rejects non-exhaustive arms, making protocol and compiler AST dispatch explicit.
CPython 3.10+ match/case: parsers and protocol adapters can select class, sequence, mapping and literal shapes with ordered guards before constructing domain values.
Scala 3 sealed ADTs and union types: the Scala compiler checks exhaustiveness while case-class patterns bind payloads for interpreters, reducers and protocol decoders.
avoid_when: The variant set is open - third-party subtypes, plugin-provided types, or a published enum you cannot seal - so no compiler can prove coverage; use polymorphic dispatch, a visitor, or a registry instead.
New variants are added frequently by other teams: every match site becomes a breaking edit; a dispatch table or subclassing absorbs that change better.
Only one variant is ever inspected and the rest are irrelevant: an optional/maybe accessor, a single type test or an if-let is simpler than a total match.
The behaviour is genuinely per-type and stable: a virtual method or the classic Visitor keeps the dispatch with the data and avoids centralising it in matches.
The data is untyped or dynamically shaped (arbitrary JSON, maps with free-form keys): decode or validate it into a typed closed set first, because patterns test structure, not invariants.
The decision is a chain of unrelated predicates rather than alternatives of one value: guard clauses, a rule engine or a specification object express it more directly.
anti_patterns: A wildcard/default arm used as the normal case, which silently disables the very check the pattern was adopted for.
Switch soup: a huge match over an open type hierarchy that re-implements polymorphism at every call site instead of dispatching on the data.
Using pattern matching as validation for untrusted input: matching a shape proves nothing about the invariants of the values inside it.
Matching on tuples of booleans and flags instead of modelling the states as a variant set, so illegal combinations remain representable.
Guard-heavy arms that smuggle conditionals into patterns and hide coverage gaps, because a guarded arm does not count as coverage for its variant.
Pattern-matching to test a condition and then rebuilding the same value by hand instead of binding the payload the pattern already extracted.
design_principles: Closed-world reasoning: the alternatives of a value are known where the type is defined, which lets the compiler prove that all of them are handled.
Make illegal states unrepresentable: each variant carries exactly the data valid for it, so matching cannot observe contradictory combinations.
Separation of data and behaviour: variant types store data, matches implement operations, and neither forces the other to change.
Fail fast: an unhandled variant should be a build error, or at worst an explicit impossible-case throw at the boundary, never a silent default.
Information hiding through binding: a pattern extracts only the fields it names, so callers never downcast or reach into representation details.
Express the expression-problem tradeoff deliberately: total matching makes new operations cheap and new variants expensive, the opposite of polymorphic dispatch.
best_practices: Keep the wildcard arm out of closed sets; where one is unavoidable for forward compatibility, put it last and make it throw rather than return a default.
Promote the coverage diagnostic to an error in CI (C# CS8509 as error, Scala E029 with warnings-as-errors, mypy exhaustive-match, a never/assertNever arm) so the check cannot be ignored.
Order arms from most specific to most general, and remember that guards do not contribute coverage, so a guarded arm rarely replaces a general one.
Extract each arm body into a named function once it exceeds a few lines, keeping the match itself a readable dispatch over the variant set.
Mark variant sets explicitly at API boundaries: non_exhaustive in Rust, @unknown default in Swift, private constructors or sealed records in C#, type aliases rather than interfaces in TypeScript.
When a variant is added, change the type first and follow the compiler errors to every match site instead of grepping for names or relying on tests.
Enforce invariants in constructors and factory functions, not inside match arms: patterns select cases, constructors make the data valid.
sources: Milner, Tofte, Harper & MacQueen, The Definition of Standard ML (Revised, MIT Press 1997) - pattern matching as a core language construct and the origin of compiler-checked case analysis.

https://softwarepatternslexicon.com/functional-programming/advanced-functional-patterns/algebraic-data-types-adts/ - functional pattern catalogue chapter on algebraic data types, where pattern matching is the eliminator of sum types.

http://web.cecs.pdx.edu/~antoy/flp/patterns/ - FLP Pattern Catalog (Antoy et al.), a functional pattern catalogue that treats pattern matching as the construct which renders several object-oriented patterns unnecessary.

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2002.06176 - Egi & Nishiwaki, Functional Programming in Pattern-Match-Oriented Programming Style (2020), whose section 3 catalogues pattern-match-oriented programming design patterns.
https://openjdk.org/jeps/441 - JEP 441, Pattern Matching for switch (Java 21): the clearest published statement of compile-time exhaustiveness over a sealed variant set.
https://smlfamily.github.io/sml97-defn.pdf - The Definition of Standard ML (SML97), the formal source for ML's datatype and pattern-matching core.
https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/reference/expressions/match-expr.html - The Rust Reference specification for match expressions, bindings, guards and exhaustive matching.
https://doc.rust-lang.org/error_codes/E0004.html - Rust's compiler diagnostic for non-exhaustive patterns.
https://peps.python.org/pep-0634/ - Python's formal specification for structural pattern matching in CPython 3.10+.
https://scala-lang.org/files/archive/spec/3.4/08-pattern-matching.html - Scala 3 specification for pattern matching, guards and exhaustiveness over sealed or union types.
https://doi.org/10.1017/s0956796807006223 - Warnings for pattern matching, an analysis of non-exhaustive and useless clauses as practical failure modes.
